headline: Trees are the longest-lived organisms on Earth—living monuments that can survive for millennia
universal_truth: Patience and persistence can outlast everything; slow and steady often wins
fun_facts: The oldest known tree is over 5,000 years old—older than the pyramids
Trees grow from the top; a mark on a trunk stays at the same height forever
A single tree can absorb 48 pounds of carbon dioxide per year
discussion_questions: What allows trees to live so long?
What could a 5,000-year-old tree tell us about history?
Why do short-lived animals seem more 'alive' than ancient trees?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: Some trees alive today were seedlings when humans invented writing. The oldest trees are over 5,000 years old—living witnesses to all of recorded history. These silent giants grow slowly, but they outlast everything.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Animals rarely live past 100 years. But trees can live for millennia. What's different about trees that allows such extraordinary lifespans?
cliff.prompt: Why can trees live so long?

options.text: Trees don't have a biological clock like animals—they can keep growing indefinitely if not killed by disease or disaster
options.response: Yes. Trees don't age the way animals do. They're modular—adding new growth while old parts die. They can theoretically live forever if nothing kills them.

options.text: Trees have slower metabolism and don't wear out as quickly
options.response: Slow metabolism helps, but the key is that trees don't have programmed aging...

q1.title: Living History
q1.script: The oldest known living tree—a bristlecone pine named Methuselah—is over 5,000 years old. It was ancient when the pyramids were built. Tree rings record climate, fires, and droughts across millennia. Trees are living archives.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Living History"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Modular Life
q2.script: Trees grow by adding new modules—new branches, leaves, roots—while old parts can die without killing the tree. This modularity means trees aren't limited by body plans like animals. They keep building themselves indefinitely.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Carbon Storage
q3.script: Trees are carbon sinks—absorbing CO2 and storing carbon in their wood. A large tree can absorb 48 pounds of carbon dioxide per year. Old-growth forests are massive carbon banks, accumulated over centuries.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Patience and persistence outlast everything. Trees teach that slow, steady growth can achieve what hurried effort cannot. Longevity comes from sustainability, not speed.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 144. Tomorrow, we'll discover why flowers exist. Until then, appreciate any tree you pass—it may have witnessed history you've only read about.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Long-Term Thinking - Plant for the Future
growTrack.activity: Consider something you could start today that would still matter in 100 years. Trees planted now will shade future generations. What 'trees' can you plant—investments in relationships, knowledge, or infrastructure that outlast you?
